BasePK: 3373665

Speech:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. It concerns a story which appeared in The Toronto Star saying that on June 17, just prior to the budget, the federal government, under the direction of the President of the Treasury Board, raised the salaries for cabinet ministers' personal staffs, special assistants, and other political appointees in their offices by at least 10 per cent. This was just prior to a budget which imposed restrictions of 6 per cent on the Public Service of Canada. Now, is that story true?
Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury
Board): Madam Speaker, perhaps I did not get the full gist of the question.

Speech:
I now
turn to the Minister of Employment and Immigration who may know that at the same time B.C. Tel is planning this very large lay-off of 2,200 people, the company will tomorrow issue a quarterly dividend of 40 cents a share, amounting to $13.4 million, going to its shareholders and to its parent company in the United States. Therefore, B.C. Tel is clearly taking advantage of bad economic times to generate even more profits at the expense of 2,200 working people.
Since the government will have to pick up the tab in unemployment insurance benefits, will the minister look into this exploitation of both the Canadian taxpayer and of his program? It is flagrant abuse of the UIC program.

BasePK: 3373996

Speech:
Madam Speaker, the national energy policy started Canada on the downhill road to disaster. Industries folded, rigs left the country, investment went elsewhere, and bankruptcies erupted. The November 12 budget was supposed to alleviate some of that distress, but it did the very opposite. It hastened bankruptcies and multiplied unemployment. Then came strike three, the June budget, and it put the icing on the cake for the destruction of Canada. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson):
18980

July 5, 1982
That this House demand the withdrawal of the November 12 budget and most of the June budget, or the immediate resignation of the minister.

BasePK: 3374094

Speech:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. The sacrificial lambs about whom he is so concerned never went through any collective bargaining process or never had any collective agreement. His comparison with the public service, let alone with the private sector which they are now asking to restrain itself, is odious at best.
If the minister feels so strongly about these sacrificial lambs, will he do two things-first, will he table a directive which he signed on June 17 and, I suggest, knowing fairly well what was in the mind of the Minister of Finance at the time in terms of his plea to other Canadians? Second, would he table the salaries of his exempt staff and of that of his colleagues over the last year so that we can see what happened last March or April with respect to wage increase for those self-same people, at the same time that he is asking every Canadian, not only public servants, to restrain themselves to 6 per cent?

I hear the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), a former minister, talking about hypocrisy. At least he does not share in the hypocrisy of his Privy Council colleagues in government because he has been thrown out of the government. I would hope that if he sat there his standards would be sufficiently high that he would not associate himself as a minister with a government which has brought in a budget so full of deceit, so full of trickery and so empty of any hope of economic recovery.
[ Translation]
I was talking about spending and restraint policies. As far as spending is concerned, this government claims that its expenditures have not increased more than 17 per cent, while in the national accounts, the government's own figures indicate an increase of 20 per cent. During the election campaign, the Liberals promised to keep the rate of government spending below the growth rate of the GNP. That is another promise they have broken, and now they are spending twice as fast as they promised to do during the campaign. As far as small businesses are concerned, the budget proudly announced a $400 million program to, and I quote:
-reduce interest costs for small businesses.
However, the program is restricted to new investment. To date, 4,500 businesses have gone bankrupt in the first five months of 1982. How many businessmen, how many farmers or fishermen, assuming they would be interested, are in a position to make new investments?

This budget is designed to deceive. It pretends to be doing things it is not doing. That pretence destroys confidence. Nobody trusts a trickster, and a budget so full of tricks and so full of deceptions is bound to destroy confidence which is key to any recovery.
Apart from trickery, what is in the budget? There is one important initiative-the introduction of restraint on public sector salaries. That is a field in which the government has lagged behind several Canadian provinces. We are relieved that it is beginning to accept that government spending is a major cause of current economic problems. As usual, its proposal is unjust. It pretends that life is as hard for a senior deputy minister as it is for a clerk or secretary, and it applies the same restraint across the board, except of course for the staff of ministers. But it is a step in the right direction toward the government admitting that its own practices affect the economy.
Beyond that, beyond imposing restraint on public servants, old age pensioners and families with children, what is the direction of this budget? What is its purpose? What philosophy or attitude inspires it? What is the government trying to do with this budget? I suggest that it is trying to do two things. First, it is trying to buy time for perhaps yet another budget in the fall or, if we can believe the President of the Treasury Board in his remarks last Wednesday and the parliamentary secretaries from Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) and Sudbury (Mr. Frith), to set the stage for wage and price controls in Canada. Apart from buying time, it is attempting to shift blame. The provinces have already been called in. No doubt big business will be called in and then the labour unions.
Anyone who has watched the confrontation tactics of this government for more than a decade will know that it is looking for someone to blame, someone to fight with, some scapegoat
July 5, 1982

to become its target and its excuse. The one area of unquestionable expertise in this government is setting up a straw man and attacking it. I would imagine that organized labour has been chosen for that role. The government wants to divert attention from its own failings and therefore it is looking for a fight with the unions. I hope that the leaders of organized labour will be wise enough not to be drawn into that trap.
Beyond buying time and shifting blame, what is the theme, the thrust, of this budget? Is it to restore confidence? With a $20 billion deficit and a hatful of tricks, is that the purpose? Is it to practise equity-that equity which was so much the siren song of the budget of last November; equity in a budget which increases taxes except for the rich; equity which singles out the elderly to pay for the government's mistakes; equity which imposes the same standard of restraint on a poor secretary in the public service as it does on a wealthy deputy minister? There is no equity in this budget.
Is its purpose to stimulate investment and thus create jobs? Obviously not when the government keeps in place the National Energy Program which has driven away billions of dollars of investment and when it offers small business, farmers, fishermen and the construction industry incentives which most of them cannot use.
The sad conclusion is that there is no purpose to this budget. There is no economic direction. This document is a short-term political response to an acute political problem. Since Liberal MPs just could not go home this summer with the government doing nothing, we have a camouflaged budget to make it appear as though the government is acting and then the subtle promise of another change in the fall.
We will see how comfortable Liberal MPs are this summer while defending a $20 billion deficit. We will see how comfortable they are defending a hidden 54 per cent increase in UIC contributions. We will see how comfortable they are this summer defending a $1.3 billion tax increase. We will see how comfortable they are defending a special plan to victimize old age pensioners. We will see how comfortable they are defending a special pay increase for the staff who work for Liberal ministers.
There is another remarkable feature of this budget, and that is the revelation that the June 28 budget did not belong to the Minister of Finance alone. It had a co-author, a co-conspirator so far unindicted. John Turner helped to write this budget. The Prime Minister smiles.

Madam Speaker, in introducing his budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) said:
The government has pointed the way to recovery, but it alone cannot get Canada on the move. We must tackle this task together.
Canada is one of the most fortunate nations in the world. We have tremendous natural resources. We have well-educated and competent workers, and we are better equipped than many countries to survive the worldwide recession. However, we want to do more than merely survive. We want to work our way out of the present difficulties in a way which leaves us well positioned to take full advantage of the upturn in the world economy when it comes.
The budget measures in themselves are worthy of serious attention, but before addressing them I would like to echo the minister's call for all Canadians to involve themselves in serious consideration of how best we can shoulder our responsibility to work our way out of current difficulties and prepare for better times.
Budget bashing is a traditional Canadian occupation. It is traditional that special interest groups respond with more and more requests to help their particular situation; it is traditional that opposition parties attack and give no credit for positive measures. In our present situation, budget bashing can easily become Canada bashing. Financial markets are skittish and respond in an exaggerated way to any evidence of political division or uncertainty.
But Canadians have a remarkable ability for compromise, for working together to overcome difficulties, for balancing the
need of regions, of minorities, of conflicting groups so as to arrive at the common good. This is a time that calls for all our goodwill and all our patriotism and pride in Canada.
Two years ago, on May 21, 1980, this House was united in a way we rarely see. Statesmanlike speeches on the Quebec referendum results were made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) and by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), and it may be useful today to remind ourselves of that spirit and of some of the statements made then.
The Leader of the Official Opposition described the referendum vote as "an expression of pride and belief in this country in which we can all joyfully share" and spoke of uniting Canadians in "a common determination to build a renewed federation which can make this a stronger country, a richer country, and a better country in years ahead".
The Leader of the New Democratic Party said:
We have ... reached a level of political maturity of which all civilized nations of the world are envious. . . . last night we showed that we can get along together despite deep differences.
Later in his speech, he said:
Fishermen in Newfoundland, farmers in Saskatchewan, miners in Sept-iles and people in every region of Canada must see the federal government as an ally, as their government. This is our objective.
The spirit which animated this House on May 21, 1980 is needed again as we face difficult times to which we can find solutions by working together.
At this time of very delicate balance, it is important that we all play a constructive role-otherwise, to quote the Financial Post, "The extreme and the implacable, egged on by the excitable in the media and unable to see merit in a middle way, may blindly help precipitate" a crisis for Canada.
Canadians are concerned about inflation, about high unemployment, about the deficit, about high interest rates; consumer, business and investor confidence are at a low ebb. To deal with all these problems requires a careful balance and mix of policies.
Most people who talk to me are more concerned about unemployment than about inflation. As long as people are working, they usually can manage in one way or another to deal with increases in the cost of living, but being unemployed takes the heart out of people. Yet we know that if inflation goes unchecked we will lose our competitive position in world markets and the long-term result will, in fact, be more unemployment. Therefore, inflation must be addressed as a high priority.
In inflationary times people try to protect themselves by negotiating higher wages, but when wages and prices chase each other, purchasing power does not increase; a 12 per cent increase does not improve the situation of a family if prices have also gone up 12 per cent.

Let us look at one which is supposed to be a jewel in the government's arsenal, the ILAP program, announced a year and a half ago, to which $350 million was allocated. It was set up supposedly to help those communities devastated by layoffs and initiate economic resurgence. Let us look at the total package the government is proposing. All of its programs together will provide 80,000 jobs this year and 84,500 jobs next year. We have 165,000 unemployed construction workers, sitting at home drawing unemployment insurance, when they want to be out working. We need a real housing program. We need to set ourselves the objective of doubling the number of houses we are building right now and building 225,000 homes in the next year. the railways, instead of hiring new people and buying new equipment, have major lay-offs. The government needs to be serious. They will be hard pressed to understand that any affirmative action programs within the public service that will be of any benefit to them will no longer be operated through the collective bargaining system, since it has been frozen by the government through this bill. Are we to think that this will contribute to the sense of fair play that the government's program is supposed to provide?
My colleague, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) talked about the national crusade and the crusaders. As we look at the national crusade of restraint we have to look at the tainted wings of the crusaders, because in the final analysis many people do not understand all of the program and the numbers, its applications and effects. For example, very few people understand that this is a bill not only dealing with restraint but one which takes away collective bargaining as well. People do not understand the consequences of the entire bill. That is why they very often do not judge by what is being said but by who is saying it; not by what is promised but by who is promising it. That is why, when it comes to the ability of the government to put through a wage restraint program in the public service, its chance of success is directly related to whether or not people regard what the government has to say as honest and believable. In short, whether or not they have any confidence in the government to carry out wage restraints.
That confidence has been undermined by government policy and government statements. For example, the fact that the deficit in the budget went up to $19.6 billion is not the most important factor. It is the fact that eight months ago the government said its deficit would be $10.5 billion. It is very difficult to have confidence in a government which makes a mistake in its understanding of the future of the economy in saying that its deficit would be $10.5 billion and it ends up at $19.6 billion. It is not only the fact that the deficit has doubled; the government could not see or did not know this would happen. It is bad enough that it doubled, but it is worse that the government did not foresee it.
The government showed its lack of leadership when it came in with a budget on November 12 which called for restraint and put its own spending at 22 per cent. It came in with its next budget on June 28, which again called for restraint and, indeed, wage restraint for the public service, when its own
July 12, 1982

spending for 1982-83 was increased by 20 per cent. People take their lead not from what is said but from what is done. This government has shown that it may be one thing for it to preach restraint but that it does entirely the opposite.
I conclude by saying that this bill is more than meets the eye. It is far less than meets expectations. It is not purely and simply a bill to restrict the wages of public servants to 6 per cent and 5 per cent. What is at stake is whether or not the government itself will be able to change in order to muster its own moral authority, which the country needs in order to have a restraint program. There is nothing wrong with restraint. There is nothing wrong with people recognizing again that the only way to progress is to exercise some frugality, and that the only way to make use of the country's natural resources is not by squandering them but by husbanding them.
While some people believe that we must exercise growth and optimism or else the belief will be that we will head in the other direction, most people in running their lives realize that if they do not look after their own resources and husband them, and if they do not discipline themselves, they will not be able to depend in the future on the bounty coming forward.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said that he is challenging Canadians. I have never heard such arrogance in my life-that we need the Prime Minister to say that his job is to challenge Canadians into restraint. Anyone who walks along the street and goes into stores, factories or shops knows that for the last two or three years people have slowly begun to change. Canadians have said, "Sure, I want more, but I know that in order to have more I must remember some of the older virtues of working hard, thrift and saving.'' They also know that much is dependent upon themselves in their communities. That is why this bill, and this Prime Minister, I might say, are not on the cutting edge of change. That is insipient arrogance which words fail me to describe.
All the government is doing is desperately trying to catch up to Canadians, who understood long ago that if there is to be any salvation for this country it depends on them and their ability to change their habits and be able to make the country work. As they watch this government they know for sure that they cannot depend on it to do either of those two things.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to make a few remarks this afternoon. A socialist of the type we just heard from is usually the guy who has nothing and wants to share it with everyone else.

The best thing we can do at the present time when things are bad is to minimize the impact of the four influences to which 1 have referred. If we can understand that we are trying to change that "What's in it for me?" attitude to an attitude of "What's in it for Canada?", we will have taken the first step on the road to recovery. Mr. Speaker, earlier today a number of members referred to the Minister of Finance as a baseball player, to their experiences in baseball, to the fact that he had been up once and struck out, up twice and struck out, up three times and should be out of the ball game, and so on. Upon reflection, although I played ball in my youth, I think a more appropriate game would be hockey. I remember watching a hockey game last winter. I will not mention the teams because what I am
about to describe is something of which I am not particularly proud. Half way through the hockey game, one player who was particularly rambunctious found himself encouraged to jump up into the stands and start beating someone over the head with his hockey stick. It was a fan who had aggravated him. Eventually the player was thrown out of the game. I suspect that that probably describes the Minister of Finance more aptly than a baseball player. He is up today with his hockey stick bashing Canadians over the head and is about to be pulled out of the game, if Canadians had an opportunity to make that decision today via a federal election.
Today we are debating Bill C-125, a bill to give the government the authority to borrow $11 billion. It must be seen in a certain context. When the Thirty-second Parliament first began, the government eventually came to Parliament asking for permission to borrow $12 billion. At that time many difficult questions were asked about how the money would be spent and so on, and hesitantly approval was eventually received. A few months later the government said that it needed another $14 billion to continue on because it was a little short; its revenues were not as much as its spending. The government needed authority to borrow another $14 billion. Then a little later it came before us again and asked permission to borrow $6.6 billion. That $6.6 billion request just received royal assent on June 17. Today, virtually four weeks later, the government has the audacity to come before Parliament and say, "Listen, we have erred in our judgment. Things have not gone quite as we expected. We are not asking for $6.6 billion this time. We are asking for $11 billion". It is asking for $11 billion only four weeks after the last request. If that does not describe a government which is out of control, if that does not support the Auditor General's claim that the economy is on its knees or the previous auditor general's comments that we are going down the tubes, I do not know what does. The government has had to come to Parliament to seek authority to borrow $43.6 billion because of its misjudgment and mismanagement of the economy. It is a sad state of affairs in the wealthiest country in the world.
If positive things had occurred as a result of this borrowing, that would have been one thing. I do not think that we can consider a 60 per cent increase in farm bankruptcies in the first six months of this year as any kind of positive program. I do not think we can consider the 37 per cent increase in business bankruptcies as any kind of positive program. I think we should be ashamed when we learn that plant capacity in the country is operating at 69 per cent of its capacity. That means there is a 30 per cent idleness in the factories of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, if we listen to the official opposition, there seems to be no end of problems in this country. I would like to say a few words about the need for amending the Small Businesses Loans Act, since Bill C-122, an act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, is extremely important at this time. First, 1 should like to say a few words on our past experience, which has in fact been quite good for small businesses, and on the financing situation, to which the member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) was referring earlier when he said that there was a considerable problem in getting lenders to offer loans to small businesses. Well, Mr. Speaker, in 1981, although there were problems, it seems the number of lenders other than chartered banks rose from 762 to 1,286. I do not know whether that could qualify as a problem, but I think there has been a good deal of progress in this area, and since the government is guaranteeing these loans, I believe that lending institutions other than banks will become more and more numerous. I should also like to say a few words about the act's historical background, the amendments made since 1961 regarding eligibility and reasons for application, and certain results which came to light during the last financial year and which were very encouraging.
The Small Businesses Loans Act came into effect in January, 1961, and its initial purpose was to encourage private lenders to provide fixed-term loans for small businesses. The act, which provides the lender with a guarantee against all losses, was initially to be effective for three years and was subsequently renewed at regular intervals. The act now in effect actually expired on June 30 of this year, and as the minister pointed out this morning, the act was to be extended for nine months so that it would expire at the same time as the legislation on loans to farmers and fishermen.
Since 1961, many amendments have been made to the act, and I shall name a few of the more important ones. In 1974, the maximum amount of loans repayable by any borrower was raised from $25,000 to $50,000 to allow for the expansion of the small business sector, an increasingly encouraging factor which required broader credit margins. In 1977, the maximum permissible loan from any lender was raised to $75,000 and the business turnover figure was raised to $1,500,000. In January, 1978, the interest rate formula was amended to allow lenders to charge prime plus 1 per cent. In 1978, responsibility for administering the act was transferred from the Department of Finance to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. In 1980, the amount of the loan offered by any lender was raised from $75,000 to $100,000. Mr. Speaker, further changes are expected, since an advisory committee has been formed to review all aspects of this legislation.
Under this legislation all Canadian chartered banks are deemed to be lending institutions. As a result of the amendments made in March, 1970, the scope of the act was enlarged

July 23, 1982
Small Businesses Loans Act (No. 3)
to include credit unions, Caisses populaires, trust companies, insurance companies and finance companies which are eligible and apply for designation by the minister. There have been many changes and those who were eligible were people in manufacturing, wholesale trade, retail trade, service businesses, communications, construction and other fields.
Naturally, there have been changes as well in the reasons why people submit applications, and loans may now be approved for purchasing real estate or movables, improving or modernizing facilities or premises, buying or building accommodation and even acquiring land. This has been a net improvement because the act has evolved with time and, as other members pointed out earlier, it will continue to evolve and to adjust to the needs of the very important small business sector. Particularly in Quebec, people are aware that small businesses play an extremely active role in our economic development and that they create hundreds of jobs. Mr. Speaker, during that short time period, under the Small Business Loans Act, 99,500 loans have been granted so far, for a total value of roughly $2 billion. In 1981 alone, 16,942 loans were approved for a total of $501,000. I have other figures which concern Quebec more particularly.
In 1981, 5,431 loans were approved as compared with 5,188 in 1980, an increase of 4.7 per cent. Even more encouraging is the fact that those loans amounted to $124 million in 1980 and about $147 million in 1981, up 18.8 per cent. Mr. Speaker, in rising today to speak to report stage of the bill, it might be worthwhile if I reminded the House of exactly what we were talking about when the bill was in second reading stage. The reason for doing so is that over the past number of days, while we have been dealing with specific amendments to the bill, much of the understanding of the principles involved has been obscured. As we come to the close of the discussion on the bill, it might be worthwhile to remind ourselves of what those principles were, how they fared during the committee stage and how it appears they will fare throughout the report stage and third reading.
There are two principles in this bill. There were two principles at first reading, two at second reading and there are still two principles. The first is the principle of restraint. During second reading I had the opportunity, as did many others in the House, to indicate, to all who were willing to listen, my views concerning whether or not it is necessary to have restraint in the economic life of the country at this time. Our party believes that there needs to be restraint at this time. We do not believe that that is all that needs to be done, either by people in the country or by the government, but it is one part of the solution. Anyone who sat throughout the committee hearings and heard economists of all stripes testify would have confirmation of one's belief in the necessity of restraint. That is why our party supports the first principle of the bill, that is, the principle of restraint.
There are some who do not believe that restraint is necessary. There are some who believe that economic growth can continue in the manner it has for the past 25 years. That is absolutely, 100 per cent wrong. The economic view held by those who argued that we can continue without the inclusion of restraint provisions as part of a package of recovery is clearly now in disrepute. Economists who offer that view and people who believe in it are fooling themselves. In my view it is irresponsible for any political party to argue in 1982 that we
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
can have economic recovery without the inclusion of restraint as part of the package of that recovery.
The second principle involved was the principle of collective bargaining. There are some who believe that we can have restraint without collective bargaining. That is the view of the government. There are some who believe we should have collective bargaining without restraint. That is the view of the New Democratic Party. Throughout the committee hearings, our whole endeavour was to arrive at a situation whereby the country could get what it needs, that is, a program of economic recovery involving restraint, while preserving a collective bargaining system which has protected the rights of people, particularly those with low income, for many years, and ensuring that those who depend on those rights can continue to depend on them throughout the two-year period of restraint.
That is why, in posing our amendment with respect to collective bargaining, we set forth the enact way in which the government ought to have gone. In a moment I will discuss why I believe the government did not take that route, although it was the most reasonable one. It makes sense to people. The amendment, as written in the Order Paper, would first of all preserve the 6 per cent and 5 per cent restraint on total compensation. It would preserve the principle of restraint. In that context, we agree with the government. Second, our amendment would have precluded the exercise of strikes during a two year period because, in our view, the program deserves the opportunity for success without the disruption caused by strikes in the public service. Quite frankly, the government has as much power as it needs because the recent Supreme Court decision gives the power to the federal government to determine what is essential and to deny the operation of the right to strike in essential services. However, since the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) sought, at every turn of the road, to bring up the bogey man of the right to strike, we agreed, and I proposed an amendment in a motion which would preclude the right to strike, with arbitration in its place. The government voted against that. Our amendment would not only have preserved the restraint of 6 per cent and 5 per cent and would not only have precluded the right to strike for the operation of the two year program, but it would also have allowed for collective bargaining when issues remained unresolved and in dispute. It would also have permitted arbitration in order to deal with unresolved issues.
That was an excellent amendment. Any fool could go along with restraint and not worry about the protection of the rights of people through collective bargaining and any fool could go along with collective bargaining while not worrying about restraint. It takes real skill, hard work and attention to detail to know that there can be both. The government should have a restraint program, not only one affecting the public service, but one which is also a beacon to other people, leading the way to restraint while not destroying 50 years of collective bargaining tradition. By adoption of that amendment, and the government still has the chance, it can do that.
That brings me to the operation of the committee. I would say at the outset that the committee was chaired by the hon.

July 30, 1982

member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). The only reason I raise that point is that although he is a Liberal member, he did an excellent job.

Mr. Speaker, I always find it amusing to listen to Conservatives speaking
about this legislation, given the fact that they intend to stand in their places and support it one by one when the final vote comes. It is hard to believe that we could have gone through three or four days of committee proceedings and then found that the bill which ultimately came back to the House of Commons was worse. The chairman of the committee is holding up his hands to indicate that it was seven days. I appreciate that. I can make that out very nicely. The problem is that no matter whether it was three, four or seven days, the days were wasted, because the legislation is now more repressive and more unacceptable than it was when it first came in.
The government, together with its friends in the Tory party, has never believed in collective bargaining. It has been first in line to restrict it every single time that restriction was called for by anyone. Its supporters, the Liberal and Conservative big business supporters, are the people who are standing up and applauding this government, saying, "Don't you worry. We will be behind you all the way. Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I understand that the minister has just tabled the government's response to the Gilson report. Instead they have merely tabled a document or issued a press release outside the House. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has demonstrated today once again his contempt and disregard for this institution and for all hon. members of the House of Commons.
This is the third occasion on which the minister has, in dealing with a question of very substantive policy, namely the future of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates in this country, avoided the House of Commons. On February 8 he issued a statement in Winnipeg and that was a substantive statement of policy. The members of the House of Commons did not have an opportunity to respond; they did not have an opportunity to question the minister or to seek clarification on a very important and complicated subject. The opposition had to use an opposition day to get this issue on the floor of the House of Commons.
On June 28 when the Gilson report was released, once again the House of Commons was circumvented. A statement was made in Winnipeg; the minister held a press conference; once again the Members of Parliament and this House of Commons were not involved.
Today we have a statement that has been tabled by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). We do not know what it contains but we do understand that it is the government's response to the report of the Gilson task force. What is further rubbing salt into the wounds of all hon. members is the fact that the minister is going to go outside of this House of Commons and hold a press conference. I believe that is contemptuous and totally disregarding the role, the responsibility and the obligations that we have as Members of Parliament. He merely tables the report today. There is no statement, no opportunity for opposition members to respond. There is no opportunity to seek clarification. He is doing it by press release by tabling a document and holding a press conference outside of this chamber.
We all know this same Minister of Transport a year ago waited until Parliament recessed to make a very substantive announcement with respect to VIA Rail. This has been a habit with this minister and I must say it has been shared as well by other ministers of this government.
I am sure that you realize, Madam Speaker, that the issue of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates is a very fundamental and important issue to the people of western Canada and particularly to the farmers, the producers and the grains industry of
western Canada. We all acknowledge that this government does not have any members in this House west of Winnipeg, but that should be no reason why this Parliament should be left out in the cold. We on this side of the House find, the action of the Minister of Transport contemptible. We believe that it constitutes an abuse of the rights and privileges of all members of this House of Commons. We believe it impairs the ability of each and every one of us to discharge our responsibility and to serve our constituents and our region.
I ask you, Madam Speaker, as one who presides over this chamber and who has the responsibility of ensuring that rights and privileges of all Members of Parliament are preserved, to seriously look into this matter and take the necessary steps to see that this practice cease and desist.

what some would have us believe about the vast wealth, in terms of income flow in any one year, of those who are termed to be rich.
Another interesting point that was raised by the Leader of the New Democratic Party concerned a new kind of industrial policy which would be put forward. In other words, those firms would pay a lower tax rate than the general corporate citizens in our country and all of those who are not considered to be industries of the future or industries that generate long-term, good jobs for Canadians would be subject to the equivalent of a surtax. Their tax would rise. The rate would go from 36 per cent federal to 46 per cent or 48 per cent federal, and if you factor in both federal and provincial taxes, a tax rate of about 62 per cent or 63 per cent would result on all of those corporations not deemed to be industries of the future; that is not worthly of encouragement.

The Leader of the New Democratic Party is saying that his party would increase taxes on firms with a very high labour content. As a result of having a high labour content in a country with high wage rates relative to some underdeveloped countries, these firms would be on the decline in Canada. Cash advances are simply moneys advanced to prairie grain producers against their future sales. They are really advances against their own products-their own money.
The federal Government comes into play because it pays the interest on the money borrowed to pay the advances. The program was initiated for this back in 1957. It is a program which has worked very well. It has put money into farmers' pockets, enabling them to pay bills sooner than they would normally pay them if they had to wait for the sale of their products. This helped the whole community because it means that having cash in advance of their sales farmers are able to pay their taxes, repair bills, fuel bills, and those kinds of ordinary expenses incurred in the normal course of operating their farms.
We all know that the economic system is a circular one. What is an expense for one person then becomes income for someone else. As it goes through the system, that money is spent over and over again. If one wants to speak in economic terms, it is called the multiplier effect. If one looks at what goes on in the farming communities, and in other communities, one finds that farmers have a greater multiplying effect than those in most other industries. It simply means that when a dollar is put into a farmer's pocket, it is used more times. The program is essentially designed to put money into the hands of those in the farming community so that they can use it to pay

their bills, and this in turn provides income to other sectors of the economy.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), I would like to speak to the House this evening about Bill C-130, an Act to authorize continuing financial assistance to be provided to certain international financial institutions. This legislation will enable the Secretary of State for External Affairs to secure, through parliamentary appropriations, the public funds earmarked for development assistance which Canada contributes through various international financial institutions. Mr. Speaker, this piece of legislation is the result of the ruling made by Madam Speaker on June 12, 1981 on a historic point of order raised about the orderly procedure with respect to certain budget items in the 1981-82 estimates.
Naturally, international financial institutions are a very significant and effective element of Canada's multilateral development assistance program. As far as this legislation is concerned, they include the four regional development banks, namely the Asian Development Bank, the African Development Bank, the InterAmerican Development Bank, the Carribean Development Bank, as well as the concessional funds pertaining to each one, and also the International Fund for Agricultural Development and the Common Fund for Commodities. Canada gives a financial contribution to each of those institutions by underwriting their share capital and/or contributing to their concessional funds. Our payments are made directly or through non-interest bearing, non-negotiable demand notes. The main reason why Canada participates in international financial institutions is that their Third World programs are effective and profitable. Those regional institutions are indeed a particularly appropriate way of promoting regional co-operation and enhancing the self-sufficiency of developing countries. The framework of capital sharing and the nature of financial co-operation among international financial institutions is an excellent example of successful cooperation in the area of development. One of the significant characteristics of our participation in those institutions is the multiplier effect of our dollars thanks to the borrowings of banks on international money markets.
In addition, this complements the other Canadian assistance programs and allows us to diversify our assistance, both geographically and sectorially, and to support the multilateral institutional framework created by these financial institutions. Canada also benefits from the standpoint of its foreign policy and especially of its trade. Our participation is one of the key elements of our relations with less developed countries and reflects the approach of the government to multilateralism and North-South relations. Moreover, Canada's membership in these institutions enables Canadian businesses to bid for certain components of projects financed by these international financial institutions in developing countries, which very often result in major economic benefits for Canada.
Financial Institutions
Mr. Speaker, I believe that this bill is relatively clear and does not call for a lengthy debate. Under clauses 2 and 4, the Governor in Council may amend the schedule, thereby adding thereto or deleting therefrom the names of the financial institutions concerned. Moreover, clause 3 provides financial assistance to these institutions by way of direct payments, demand notes and the purchase of shares. Section 5 states that the sums required for the purposes of the Act must be approved by Parliament and limited to amounts appropriated. Section 6 provides for an interim appropriation valid until presentation of the Main Estimates, next Spring. These sums cover the following investments: the fourth and last payment in respect of the fourth general increase in the capital of the InterAmerican Development Bank, or an amount of $7,290,000, and the fourth payment in respect of the third general increase in the capital of the Caribbean Development Bank, which represents $883,000, as well as the following payments: the first, fourth and last payment in respect of the third reconstitution of the Asian Development Fund for an amount of $56,722,000; the fourth and last payment in respect of the fifth reconstitution by the InterAmerican Development Bank of its Fund for Special Operations for an amount of $18,156,000; a contribution to the Special Development Fund of the Caribbean Development Bank in the amount of $531,000, and finally, the first payment in respect of the third reconstitution of the African Development Fund for an amount of $33,900,000. Except for the payments to the Caribbean Development Bank, all these appropriations will be in the form of notes.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I want to remind the House that some of these allocations are necessary to meet the immediate commitments of Canada to the institutions concerned. This is why I invite my colleagues to act urgently in this regard because if Parliament delays too much or if we are victims of a filibuster by the Opposition so that this bill is not passed before December 31, Canada will not be able to meet its commitment to increase its Development Aid Program to .5 per cent of the GNP by 1985. I know that the Hon. Member for New West-minster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett) is very anxious for Canada not only to reach this figure of .5 per cent, but also to exceed it, and I ask for her co-operation and for the co-operation of the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) so that we may meet our international obligations. With this in mind, Mr. Chairman, I hope that the debate will be enlightening, but mostly, I hope it will be brief.

Speaker, yesterday the Government and the Official Opposition agreed to adjourn the House of Commons after Remembrance Day eulogies, as a special tribute to our fallen comrades. I am very disappointed that the New Democratic Party refused to participate in that gesture to honour those who

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on today's motion which reads:
That this House, recognizing the importance of providing efficient, affordable, equitable mail service to all Canadians, and recognizing that Canada Post has reduced service while increasing its rates, condemns the Government for its failure to enforce the provisions of the Canada Post Corporation Act which require Canada Post to provide Canadians with adequate service at a reasonable cost.
This is a motion which I, and I believe the people of Canada, welcome.
1 would first like to say to the Minister, in particular, that my colleagues and I in this Party will be responsible. In being responsible, we will not attack the Canada Post Corporation nor the new management of that Corporation. Unlike the irresponsibility shown by Liberals and Conservatives in the House and across the country, irresponsibility which they have shown in numerable occasions, we will not attack the employees of the Corporation, whether they be inside workers or outside workers. We in the NDP want the Government, the Official Opposition and especially the Minister also to be responsible. In this respect I could not help but think that he sounded like the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) who, during a recent debate in the House, appeared so sensitive to attacks on his poor administration that he tried to pretend that Opposition Members, whether Tories or from the NDP, were attacking the employees of the Unemployment Insurance Commission instead of the policies of the Minister. Similarly, this Minister's policy towards the post office has left it with little alternative but to do the damage that is being done.
The result of the entire administration of Canada Post today has been some improvement to urban services, while there is a reduction in service, poorer service and I would suggest almost a sabotage of service in rural Canada. The effect the Government has had on the Canada Post Corporation as a result of the Minister's policies is typical of what happens when you give any city slicker lawyer the responsibility for essential services to rural Canada.
This is similar to the problem which was faced by VIA Rail after its services were separated. It was given an impossible mandate, starved of funds and resources and the passenger service was separated from the freight service which financially carried it. This same situation is happening to the post office, whereby the Government will likely eventually decide that the service to rural Canada has become uneconomic. It will build up a large public blacklash, especially from some of the private sector, which will then demand to be allowed to cream off those portions of the postal service which are
profitable and then leave the remaining Canadians, particularly those in the hinterland areas of Canada, with no service or with service at excessive cost which they cannot honestly be expected to bear.
I admit from the outset that there have been improvements in the Canada Post Corporation. One of these improvements has been an increase in mail delivered "on time" from approximately 80 per cent to 89 per cent during the last year. That is a significant improvement over a relatively short period. That is one of very few improvements. We have also seen many other basic services threatened.
I want to express my consternation and surprise at the Conservative Party for proposing a motion such as this. It takes a lot of nerve and even more hypocrisy for them to do this. The Conservatives have given their support to, and in fact called for many of the policies that the Government has agreed to follow-since the Government is acting like Tories so often-and that are causing the problems that exist within the Canadian postal service. 1 am amazed at the gall shown by those who proposed this motion when I consider what they have done previously.
Only a year ago we in the NDP, along with most Members from all Parties and certainly the vast majority of Canadians, were at least hopeful, if not optimistic, that the birth of the Canada Post Corporation, which had been demanded by so many for so long, could be a genuine rebirth of a once proud and efficient servant of the Canadian people. I say "hopefull" and not "optimistic" because we had some grave doubts due to what we believed to be the straitjacket of the unrealistic timetable of total and early self-imposed restraint and financial self-sufficiency which was demanded by the Government and supported by the Conservatives. The Government and those Members of the Official Opposition who sponsored the Government's policy were not satisfied with shackling this infant Corporation with the impossible demand of short-term self-sufficiency. They proceeded to starve it and batter it with the six and five program while hypocritically demanding that this infant Corporation rush to premature maturity and provide proper service to Canadians.
Let us examine what exactly was done. Michael Warren, President of Canada Post Corporation, has continually spelled out the three primary goals of the Corporation, as provided for under the Canada Post Corporation Act. The first goal is improved service; the second is improved human relations; the third is financial self-sufficiency. In the budget of November 12, 1981, a couple of budgets and one economic statement ago, the then Minister of Finance very clearly laid out the Government's expectations for financial self-sufficiency. From 198182, the Government expects the Canada Post Corporation to reduce its deficit of $620 million to zero by the year 1985-86. That is quite a demand at a time when the Government, the Official Opposition and this party are also apparently and hopefully committed to at least providing efficient and improved service across the country.

need of individual Canadians and small businessmen. What is a more efficient postal service? Our response would be a service which provides a basic customary postal service to the greatest possible number of Canadians, whether they live on the prairies or the far North, or an individual in northern Manitoba.
Let me digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to deal very briefly with some of the arguments advanced during this debate and earlier in committee when we were passing the legislation to establish the Crown Corporation.
We have the argument that the Government and the post office were being too restrictive in their definition of a letter. The argument was advanced that we should not restrict the definition of a letter; we need more competition. Those people who say that, Mr. Speaker, are doing a great disservice to Canadians, particularly to Canadians who live in the bigger cities of this country. If you got the so-called competition which some of the banks and other commercial organizations want, Mr. Speaker, you would have those organizations skimming off the easy and cheap to deliver mail in the big cities. What would be left for the post office? All the difficult mail, all the rural and isolated areas where the cost to deliver mail is very expensive. Then you would get the argument that the Postal Corporation could not afford to provide the kind of service it has been providing until now. You would get further cutbacks in service in the rural and isolated areas, as we have had cutbacks in VIA rail service. So we say that we want the post office to be efficient and able to deliver mail quickly, without the mistakes which have happened before.
However, Mr. Speaker, we do not believe that efficiency means subsidizing corporate business structure, which is interested in selling its goods by getting a subsidy from the people of Canada. We believe that a step in the right direction for the kind of program I have talked about would be a clear definition of what basic customary postal service really means.
I say to the Minister that it means, in the cities and suburbs of Canada, door-to-door delivery. It does not mean delivery to letter boxes in suburban areas which may be a mile or more from where people live. We had that situation right into the 1979 election. The fact that an election was looming is what got the Government to agree to the hiring of more letter carriers. 1 do not know whether it is going to need another election, but we need to get the kind of door-to-door service to the suburbs that the cities have had for many years. I consider myself still to be a new Member in terms of Standing Orders, even though I was elected to this House in 1979. November 29, 1982
Adjournment Debate
matter as to most others relating to his constituency. I am quite pleased to announce that the project is now being carried out after several years of hard work devoted to planning and negotiations. The planning activities were spread out over a number of years because of the extent and complexity of that development project and the need to secure the participation of many interested parties of both the public and private sectors.
Our aim was to revitalize the eastern section of the National Capital, create permanent jobs and opportunities for the construction industry, as well as promote the use of vacant land belonging to the federal Government. I am convinced that the Crown will derive financial returns from its share of the gross revenue of the project.

What matters, Mr. Speaker, is that the project will have created approximately 2,000 jobs in construction operations on Canadian Government land between 1981 and 1983, 1,000 jobs in the general building industry in the National Capital Region, and additional jobs in the service industries. Mr. Speaker, the participation of the Federal Government is as follows: Department of Public Works, $19 million, and National Capital Commission, $11 million; the very significant participation of the private sector and the other levels of government is approximately $173 million.

That quote stands on the record.

Mr. Speaker, the topic we are discussing today has already been the subject of many a debate. It seems this is the fifth time a motion of this kind is being proposed. I must admit that, initially, I would be inclined to agree that perhaps more information should be accessible to Canadians, on a wider variety of subjects-I would almost say on just about everything. 1 do not think this is feasible. With the previous speakers, I deplore this, but at the same time 1 understand there are some things that can and others that cannot be said.
When it is said that the information requested cannot be provided because of confidentiality as understood in Section 14 of the Foreign Investment Review Act, and that such information may not be disclosed without the explicit consent of the parties who provided the information to the Government, it seems to me, first of all, that the Government must observe any undertaking it has made. I also think that the confidentiality of transactions that have already been examined and submitted for approval to the Foreign investment Review Agency, must be preserved, if only to protect the companies themselves, for obvious reasons which include the existence of competitors and the possibility of plagiarism, and so on. This is not to say that in the long run, Section 14 should not be amended in some way to enable Members, and therefore all Canadians, to be better informed. Ffowever, as regards relations between private companies who are already being asked to submit very confidential information, to see whether their intended investment in Canada will benefit Canadians when the Agency has made a decision, I feel that any commitments made to these companies must be met, and that if we decide to admit them as entrepreneurs in Canada, we must realize that a commitment has been made not to disclose information they have submitted.
As for certain Crown corporations to which my colleagues referred, I think a clear distinction should be made between the private company which establishe commercial relations and Crown corporations which are subject to certain regulations that could certainly be the subject of discussion or debate. However, 1 do not want to give the impression that 1 am particularly well informed as a backbencher. On the other hand, I think that the appropriate time for discussing the matter of being better or more fully informed is certainly not when a motion is being proposed regarding commercial transactions between two private companies which submitted their applications for scrutiny by the Foreign Investment Review Agency. I would have liked to hear a far more extensive debate regarding Crown corporations which operate with funds allocated to them by the Government of Canada.
I am not as sympathetic to the motion before the House, which asks the Government to publish information submitted in good faith to a Government agency that has extensive responsibilities and which, I feel, is acting very responsibly, and towards which the Government was bound not to disclose this information. Where the Member of the New Democratic Party referred to the Foreign Investment Review Agency, saying that during the last election campaign, a commitment was made to amending the regulations in the interest of Canadians, I think it is in the interest of Canadians that not all information should be made public. If we want a company to be interested in getting established in Canada, we should by all means create conditions that are favourable to such a move. If one of those conditions is to respect commitments to these companies that submit documents for consideration, something we have a right to demand, Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that in the final instance, these companies will become new corporate citizens. The Government does not give me the right to demand what the intentions of these companies are in coming to Canada. What we want to know is whether these companies will be good corporate citizens and whether they will operate for the benefit of Canada. I think that is what FIRA is doing. Now, if we feel that the powers vested in FIRA are exaggerated or too extensive, this should be clearly indicated in a motion. It seems to me, however, that in the present case which concerns transactions between Redpath Industries Limited and the other companies mentioned in the motion, these transactions do not warrant a motion of this kind nor an amendment to Section 14. As I said before, I would have preferred to see a debate on areas or companies for which we are responsible and which we ourselves created under an Act of Parliament.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, till further notice, I shall certainly have to speak out against this motion as it is formulated, but I agree that while certain things should be said, they are not. Unfortunately, this motion is not the proper vehicle for changing this state of affairs.

In the Christmas story as it was told by Dickens over 100 years ago, he outlined the problems of his age, but he did it in the course of a story about a Christmas Day in England. He was a critic of the free enterprise system of the times and he demonstrated that system through the person of Scrooge. He indicated the people who were making the money for Scrooge through the family of Cratchitt; and the little crippled boy, Tim Cratchitt, who was part of the Cratchitt family, represented the poor, the weak, the outcasts of society in England at that time.
During this time the Members of the House of Commons and many people across Canada will rejoice again in the story. It is a great parable. It is done in modern literature, it is done on television, it is done as a movie, but basically it was a parable about the disparity which existed in English life 140 years or 150 years ago. In this week just prior to Christmas we are playing out in another form part of that story. We have around us the great evils of recession and unemployment which are biting into and injuring the families of so many Canadians, but here in the House of Commons we are discussing Family Allowances; one of the basic ways in which families can stay

part and parcel of Canadian life, and this Bill is going to cut back in a regressive way the income of Canadian families.

They are the ones we are talking about today. These are the ones who will have to plan the pension plans for you and me and for a lot of other people. At a time like this it is important that our children understand the importance of having all sectors of society well looked after, beginning with them. If you worked in a coal mine or factory at that time, you received a certain income. It was only then that people in Government decided that that injustice really could not continue, that there would have to be some kind of a social system so that children, people who did not have a job, the aged and the sick would be looked after no matter what happened in the economic system. That happened because of visionaries, people who saw that the economic system could not address the problems of all people.

Title: Energy Costs and Fertilizer Prices During the Eighties
Background: Fertilizer is becoming one of the most important and costly inputs in the crop production sector of agriculture. Farm sector expenditures for fertilizer has increased by 620 per cent for the period 1971 to 1981 and now exceeds $ 1 billion annually. There has also been an increase in terms of fertilizer's share of total farm operating expenses. Before the dramatic rise in energy prices in 1973, fertilizers accounted for approximately 5.5 per cent of operating expenses. In 1981, this figure had increased to 9.4 per cent.
While potash and phosphate fertilizer materials are refined from mineral deposits, nitrogen fertilizers are manufactured with natural gas being the originating feedstock. With rising costs for natural gas and other energy inputs required for its manufacturing, the price of nitrogen containing fertilizers will continue to escalate during the rest of this decade. With increased agricultural production targets being a part of Canada's agri-food strategy, and higher nitrogen application rates being one immediately practical way of achieving this goal, it is imperative that price projections and anticipated levels of supply should be available for the information of both the fertilizer industry, the farming community and government analyses. Such information would be required by the Directorate for presentation at the annual Outlook Conference.
Requirements: The final report should contain information on the following:
(1) North American nitrogen fertilizer capacity. The location, capacity and level of technology used for both existing and new plants presently under construction or
expansion should be included. (2) Energy inputs required for production. A section on the various direct energy inputs required for the production of a tonne of ammonia and urea and their relative importance in overall production costs. (3) Price projections for energy inputs. The latest available price projections for natural gas, electricity and other energy inputs required for the production process. (4) Trading patterns for nitrogen fertilizers. A regional accounting of trans-border nitrogen fertilizer movements. (5) Supply and demand projections for nitrogen fertilizers. The emphasis should be on the North American supply and demand situation but some projections on the world situation is also warranted. On a Canadian level, projections should be on a regional basis as well as nationally.
(6) Nitrogen fertilizer price projections. Only ammonia and urea prices need to be considered as these are the major nitrogen fertilizer materials.
Methodology: The proposed methodology for determining future levels of supply and demand is to use a simplistic approach rather than a full scale econometric model. A number of regression equations should be developed which use presently available data series and the most recent price projections to determine the probable course of future fertilizer prices.
Relevant reports which can provide guidance and/or information in completing this study include: (1) Challenge for Growth, (2) Global 2000, (3) Canada West Foundation, (4) FAD and OECD food production projections.
In addition to the pure statistical work, there should be a close linkage to the fertilizer industry. The issues addressed are of vital concern to individual companies and some of the larger corporations have personnel involved in this area. Close cooperation is seen as a way of avoiding duplication of effort and improve the quality and relevance of the results.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, welcome the opportunity of being able to participate in this most important debate. It is something 1 really do not enjoy, however, because of the fact that I find Bill C-133 to be one of the most repugnant pieces of legislation to be introduced in the House since I have been here.
As speaker after speaker from both opposition parties has indicated, this Bill is breaking a contract between the Government and its past and present employees. It destroys an agreement, something which would not be allowed in the private sector. It is morally and economically wrong. Essentially what it does is cap at the 6.5 per cent and 5.5 per cent level the increase in pensions of some 154,367 retired public servants who receive an average pension of some S6,900 a year. They will receive an increase in their pension of 0.5 per cent more than mothers or people on Old Age Security because of a sense of guilt by the Government over the fact that these people have paid into a fund and are indeed entitled to full indexation because they won it in contract negotiations.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Government can claim that the net effect is not going to be all that great because inflation is going to be down next year, perhaps even to 6 per cent. We all hope it will be, but that is not the point. The point is that retired civil servants have fought for and won the right to some protection in periods of rapid economic change. They have paid for it. There is no guarantee, Mr. Speaker, of what the inflation rate will be during the next two years. When we look at the economic forecasts during the last two years, what sticks out is that nobody knows what in heaven's name is going on. All the predictions have been wrong-predictions as to what is happening with the economy, when the recovery is going to occur, what Government deficits are going to be, what inflation or unemployment is going to be. Economists, both in the private and public sector, have been unable to make any accurate, long-term predictions. No one can tell us with any degree of certainty what the inflation rate is going to be next year, yet Bill C-133 removes the protection against inflation for the very people who need that protection the most. The
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
only protection people such as mothers or the retired have is what they have legally gained through institutions such as Parliament. But the Government removes this protection in the name of fighting inflation. That is insanity and cynicism from the Government opposite which just amazes me. It is wrong economics.
The Conference Board of Canada stated last week, and I quote from The Globe and Mail of January 13, 1983:
-the recovery will continue to be hampered by the weak growth expected in real disposable income in 1983.
Essentially the Board says that while consumer confidence is high in Canada, the ability of Canadians to purchase the goods and services they want and need is hampered by the fact that they do not have the purchasing power, and the cutbacks introduced by the Government and massive unemployment are preventing economic recovery. This proposed legislation, Mr. Speaker, further aggravates the basic problem. We are not going to get on the road to economic recovery with legislation like Bill C-133. In fact, this Bill further slows down the economy. I am not certain that there is an explanation for why the Government cannot see or understand this. Perhaps it does. Perhaps it is quite willing cynically to say: "This is the price we are prepared to pay to wrestle inflation to the ground. We are prepared to see old age pensioners, mothers, and retired civil servants squeezed even further in order to fight inflation to the ground."
We in the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker, have maintained from day one that this type of Reaganomics will not work. The amount of human suffering is too great to make this an acceptable cure for inflation. In fact, this type of Reaganomics will lead to economic disaster, bankruptcies, massive unemployment and, perhaps, to the very ruin and crash of our present economic system.
I was definitely encouraged to hear Members of the Conservative Party denounce this legislation because it broke contracts. They spoke in terms of the importance of understanding and of gentlemen's agreements on contracts. They are absolutely correct, but I sense a bit of a double standard there because they supported Bill C-124 which capped salaries of public servants. That Bill broke a lot of contracts that had been negotiated between public servants and their employer, the Government, yet we only heard two Members of the Conservative Party protest that obnoxious Bill C-124.
I think the Conservative Party still has a chance to show how sincere its opposition is to Bills C-131, 132 and 133. Members will meet in convention next week. I challenge them to introduce and pass a resolution at that convention that would denounce Bills C-131, C-132 and C-133. If at that convention they pass resolutions condemning those pieces of legislation, then some of the faith that I used to have in that Party will be restored. I challenge its Members to introduce such a motion and to marshal it through the convention next week.

January 18, 1983

I believe that these two old Parties want to reduce indexing and eventually have no indexing, in spite of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) believed a few years ago.
Every Canadian would be willing to co-operate in fighting inflation and providing employment. We will do what we can to prevent this legislation from passing.
Even with a modest amount of inflation, or even zero inflation, the necessity for an increase in pension will still arise to allow for an increase in the standard of living. However, we will not likely reach that stage for some time.
1 would remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the legislation with which we are confronted is reminiscent of former policies. I invite my friends on the Government side and in the Official Opposition to go back and read Hansard of 1929 and through the "Dirty Thirties". We are now into our 116th year of Confederation and we have had nothing but Grits and Tories and Tories and Grits, booms and busts, depressions and booms and recessions and busts. It is a vicious circle.
It is interesting to consider that this legislation attacks the pensions of former federal employees whose pensions were part of their wage package. Every government or private employer has taken into account the expenditures it has had to make for unemployment insurance premiums, workmen's compensation and its share of pension deductions as part of the wage package. Since it was considered as part of the wage package, private sector employers were able to add that to their cost of doing business. Working people considered deductions for a pension as part of the wages they earned in all the years they were employed. It is their money and not the Government's to make use of. That is money which the Government holds in trust for federal civil service pensioners.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak against Bill C-133, and particularly this amendment, which is an insult.
I agree with the concept of Government restraint. The record shows that we voted in favour of the restraint program of the federal Government. I would like to make it perfectly clear now that the vote was not also a vote in favour of breaking faith with the many public service pensioners who will be affected by Bill C-133. I find it very disturbing that, as part of the federal Government's so-called restraint program, it has decided to penalize public sector pensioners. 1 am deeply concerned that this Government, reversing its repeated promise for a just and equitable tax system, is now adopting a proposal which clearly discriminates against a segment of the population who are the most susceptible to the vagaries of this recession-wracked economy, elderly pensioners.
Indexation of our tax system affords taxpayers a measure of protection against inflation and at the same time imposes a degree of financial discipline and spending control of the federal Treasury. With this proposal, the Government will profit from inflation through the erosion of the income of civil service pensions. No incentive will exist for this Government to try to halt the inflation spiral. Unlike those Canadians who, despite Liberal policies, are working, pensioners are not able to negotiate increases to their incomes to help them cope with rising costs. That is why the fully indexed pension is so necessary. It enables men and women on fixed incomes to keep the purchasing power they have when they retire. The argument that the universal old age pension goes equally to the well-off as to the needy elderly, does not apply. The very needy elderly are eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, which continues to be fully indexed. The well-off elderly are in a fortunate position. However, there are about 100,000 elderly recipients of universal old age pensions whose outside incomes are just barely above the $6,000 cut-off for the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
The Senate of Canada maintains that a two-person family earning less than $11,030 in 1980, a figure which must be higher now considering this Government's track record of recessionary policies, live in abject poverty. Former public sector workers and their survivors currently receive an average of only $6,900 per year. In large cities, pensioners live well below the poverty line. While $55 may not seem to be a large amount of money, to many pensioners who have planned for their retirement, next year this amount will be very important.

Madam Speaker, during this harsh economic time it is especially significant to note that Canada stands alone among the major industrialized nations in that it does not have some form of national productivity centre.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated in his three talks to the nation, improvement in the country's economy, especially in regard to our international trading position, requires, in part, an improvement in Canadian productivity.
